title: Ghana’s preferential tariff access shifts export competition toward non-tariff compliance and traceability capacity
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11471, An Analysis of Ghana’s Good Export Market Access
geography: Ghanaian exports to seven major destinations: China, European Union, India, South Africa, Switzerland, United Arab Emirates, and United States

observations.period: Ghana export market access; latest available tariff and non-tariff-measure data across seven major destinations

tariff_access.value: Ghana benefits from low or zero tariffs in several developed markets through preferential and unilateral preference schemes; EU, Switzerland, and United States tariffs are near zero for Ghanaian products in the reported comparison

overall_ntm_trade_value.value: 87% of Ghana’s trade value is subject to at least one non-tariff measure across the partner-country comparison

agriculture_ntm_frequency.value: agricultural goods face approximately 100% non-tariff-measure frequency in the main export markets
agriculture_ntm_frequency.unit: percent of agricultural product lines covered

access_conversion.value: formal tariff preference does not automatically become usable market access; exporters must convert it through standards, testing, conformity, labeling, and documentation capacity

observations.method: Descriptive analysis of tariffs from WITS/TRAINS and non-tariff measures from UNCTAD datasets, by destination, product, sector, frequency, and trade-weighted coverage.
observations.uncertainty: Tariff and NTM coverage measures do not establish whether each measure is binding, protectionist, welfare-improving, or actually caused an export failure; datasets use different years and product classifications.
observations.subgroup: Ghanaian agricultural and mining exporters, smaller firms, cocoa and nuts producers, importing consumers, regulators, certifiers, and workers in export-linked supply chains.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some SPS and technical measures protect consumers, improve product quality, or enable premium markets; compliance can create capability and trust rather than only a barrier.

observations.period: Ghana agricultural exports; cocoa, cocoa products, coconuts, and cashews facing SPS and technical barriers

denominator.unit: agricultural product groups highlighted in the paper’s market-access analysis

required_capabilities.value: market access requires product conformity, quality standards, testing, labeling, and related sanitary and phytosanitary compliance

small_firm_burden.value: smaller firms may be limited from export markets because they lack capacity to meet often-high compliance costs

product_concentration.value: Ghana’s agricultural export exposure includes cocoa beans, cocoa paste and butter, coconuts, and cashews, with specific barriers varying by destination and product

firm_selection.value: the effective market-access regime can select for firms able to finance testing, certification, data, and traceability even when tariffs are low

observations.method: Product- and destination-level tariff, SPS, and technical-barrier comparisons, with frequency and coverage ratios and discussion of compliance capability.
observations.uncertainty: The paper does not estimate the number of firms excluded, compliance costs per firm, export-entry effects, or the welfare effects of each measure; small-firm impacts are a supported risk and research agenda.
observations.subgroup: Small and large exporters, farmer organizations, processors, certifiers, informal and formal producers, workers, and consumers concerned with food safety and environmental standards.
observations.counterinterpretation: Shared compliance infrastructure, producer cooperatives, public testing, and premiums can reduce fixed costs and allow smaller producers to participate; exclusion is not inevitable.

observations.period: Ghana cocoa exports to the European Union; EU Deforestation Regulation and national traceability response

denominator.unit: reported implementation components: farm-level traceability and farmer-family integration

eu_dependence.value: approximately 60% of Ghana’s cocoa products are absorbed by the European Union

eudr_requirement.value: EU Regulation 2023/1115 requires deforestation-free compliance for cocoa shipments entering the EU, making farm-to-port tracing materially relevant to market access

farm_mapping.value: Ghana has digitally mapped more than 1 million farms using GPS and polygon mapping, according to the paper’s cited policy discussion

farmer_integration.value: more than 800,000 farm families are being integrated into a digital system; Ghana is seeking a 200-dollar-per-ton sustainability premium to cover traceability and sustainable-production costs
farmer_integration.unit: farm families and dollars per ton

digital_governance_route.value: environmental market access is becoming a data, identity, and verification infrastructure question as well as a tariff question

observations.method: Policy and regulatory discussion linked to Ghana Cocoa Traceability System, national farm mapping, farmer registration, sustainability-premium proposals, and EUDR requirements.
observations.uncertainty: The paper reports implementation claims and policy direction rather than independently evaluating mapping completeness, farmer inclusion, premium receipt, data governance, or whether compliance preserves smallholder market access.
observations.subgroup: Cocoa farmers and households, smallholders without digital access, COCOBOD, exporters, EU consumers, certifiers, forest communities, and firms financing traceability.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital traceability can improve services, environmental accountability, farmer identity, and premium capture if data rights, costs, and benefit distribution are credible; it can also shift compliance burdens downward.

related_sources.claim: Official World Bank record, WPS number, authors, date, abstract, Ghana geography, and document metadata.
World Bank document API record containing the official PDF URL, abstract, report number, authors, and document identifier.

boundary: This record adds a tariff-preference-to-compliance-infrastructure mechanism. It is descriptive market-access and regulatory evidence, not proof that NTMs caused export exclusion, that compliance improves farmer welfare, or that digital traceability is complete, trusted, or fairly compensated. Small-firm exclusion, farmer burden, consumer benefit, and political accountability require firm-, farmer-, household-, and implementation-level follow-through.
